title: Prerequisites & Math
blurb: The math you actually need to understand AI engineering. Enough to read papers, enough to debug models — and a meta-node on how much is enough so you don't get stuck here.

nodes.label: Linear algebra
nodes.description: Vectors, matrices, the four fundamental subspaces, eigenvalues, SVD, matrix decompositions. The mental model behind every weight matrix, embedding, and attention computation in modern AI.
nodes.doneWhen: You can describe what an SVD does and why low-rank decompositions matter for LoRA and PCA.

resources.title: Essence of Linear Algebra
resources.author: Grant Sanderson (3Blue1Brown)
resources.annotation: The visual intuition for vectors, matrices, and eigenstuff. Watch this before any textbook.

resources.title: MIT 18.06 — Linear Algebra (OCW)
resources.author: Gilbert Strang
resources.annotation: The classic university course with full video lectures. Pair with 3Blue1Brown for intuition first, rigor second.

resources.title: Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra (VMLS)
resources.author: Boyd & Vandenberghe
resources.annotation: Free PDF. The applied view — least-squares-centric, engineering-flavored. The right book if you want LA for ML, not for pure math.

resources.title: Mathematics for Machine Learning
resources.author: Deisenroth, Faisal, Ong
resources.annotation: Free PDF. The linear-algebra chapters cover exactly what ML practitioners need, scoped to ML examples throughout.

nodes.label: Calculus (derivatives & gradients)
nodes.description: Derivatives, partial derivatives, gradients, the chain rule, Jacobians. The chain rule is the engine of backpropagation; you should be able to derive it on a whiteboard.
nodes.doneWhen: You can hand-derive the gradient of a simple two-layer network's loss with respect to its weights.

resources.title: Essence of Calculus
resources.author: Grant Sanderson (3Blue1Brown)
resources.annotation: Same visual treatment as Essence of Linear Algebra; derivatives and the chain rule made concrete in two hours.

resources.title: Khan Academy — Multivariable Calculus
resources.annotation: Problem-driven, free, the standard 'fill in the gaps' resource for partial derivatives and gradient intuition.

resources.title: Matrix Calculus for Deep Learning
resources.author: Parr & Howard
resources.annotation: The bridge from scalar calculus to the matrix-shaped derivatives that show up in every backprop derivation.

nodes.label: Probability & statistics
nodes.description: Random variables, distributions, expectation, variance, conditional probability, Bayes' rule, MLE, hypothesis testing, the basics of estimators. The language of every ML loss function and every evaluation report.
nodes.doneWhen: You can read a results table with confidence intervals and explain what the numbers mean.

resources.title: Harvard Stat 110 — Probability
resources.author: Joe Blitzstein
resources.annotation: Free lectures plus the famous Probability Cheatsheet. The gold-standard intro: rigorous and oddly entertaining.

resources.title: MIT 6.041 — Introduction to Probability (OCW)
resources.annotation: MIT's intro probability with full videos, problem sets, and rigorous treatment of distributions and limit theorems.

resources.title: Think Stats (2e)
resources.author: Allen Downey
resources.annotation: Free book. Computational statistics taught in Python — the right book if you learn by coding rather than proving.

nodes.label: Optimization
nodes.description: Convex vs non-convex, gradient descent variants, line search, second-order intuition (Newton, quasi-Newton), why deep learning's loss landscape is weird. The training-time view of every model.
nodes.doneWhen: You can explain why SGD with momentum often beats plain gradient descent and where Adam fails.

resources.title: Convex Optimization
resources.author: Boyd & Vandenberghe
resources.annotation: The reference. Free PDF. The convex half is the prerequisite for understanding why non-convex deep-learning loss landscapes are hard.

resources.title: An overview of gradient descent optimization algorithms
resources.author: Sebastian Ruder
resources.annotation: Survey of SGD / momentum / Adam / RMSprop with intuition for when each one wins. Older but still the canonical reference.

resources.title: Why Momentum Really Works
resources.author: Gabriel Goh
resources.annotation: Interactive Distill article that makes momentum geometrically obvious in 10 minutes.

nodes.label: Information theory basics
nodes.description: Entropy, cross-entropy, KL divergence, mutual information. The currency of every loss function in modern AI and the basis of compression-flavored arguments about learning.
nodes.doneWhen: You can derive cross-entropy loss from KL divergence and explain why it's the standard classification objective.

resources.title: Visual Information Theory
resources.author: Christopher Olah
resources.annotation: The single best intro post: entropy, KL divergence, cross-entropy, all made visual. Read once and the formulas stop being magic.

resources.title: Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms
resources.author: David MacKay
resources.annotation: Free PDF of the classic textbook. The rigorous treatment when you want to go deeper than Olah's overview.

nodes.label: Numerical methods & floating point
nodes.description: Floating-point representations (FP32, FP16, BF16, FP8), numerical stability, log-sum-exp, gradient explosion, mixed precision. What actually happens when a model trains on a GPU.
nodes.doneWhen: You can explain why softmax is computed via log-sum-exp and what BF16 trades off vs FP16.

resources.title: What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic
resources.author: David Goldberg
resources.annotation: The classic primer. Read once, keep handy. Old but the IEEE 754 fundamentals haven't moved.

resources.title: PyTorch Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP)
resources.annotation: The actual reference for FP16 / BF16 in training and inference. The documentation reads as a tutorial.

resources.title: NVIDIA Mixed-Precision Training User Guide
resources.annotation: How GPUs actually do mixed precision — Tensor Cores, loss scaling, the practical gotchas. Pair with the PyTorch AMP docs.

nodes.label: Discrete math (graphs & combinatorics)
nodes.description: Graphs, trees, combinatorics, basic algorithms — the CS-fundamentals layer that's useful for tokenization, retrieval, and the algorithmic side of AI systems. Skip if your CS background already covers it.
nodes.doneWhen: You're comfortable thinking about retrieval, search, and graph-flavored algorithms.

resources.title: MIT 6.042J — Mathematics for Computer Science (OCW)
resources.author: Leighton, Meyer
resources.annotation: The standard CS-foundations course. Right depth if you're filling in CS-1xx gaps before getting to algorithms.

resources.title: Algorithms Illuminated
resources.author: Tim Roughgarden
resources.annotation: A four-volume gentle re-introduction to algorithms. Useful for the retrieval and search-flavored parts of AI systems.

nodes.label: How much math is enough?
nodes.description: A meta-node addressing the most common anxiety: 'do I need to master measure theory before I touch a transformer?' Short answer: no. Be able to read papers and debug models; you don't need to prove convergence theorems.
nodes.doneWhen: You stop deferring AI work because you 'don't know enough math' and start the next stage.

resources.title: Mathematics for Machine Learning
resources.author: Deisenroth, Faisal, Ong
resources.annotation: Free PDF. The scoped middle ground: more than Khan Academy, less than a real-analysis textbook. Read this and you have enough.

resources.title: A Recipe for Training Neural Networks
resources.author: Andrej Karpathy
resources.annotation: Not strictly about math — the spirit of the answer. Deep ML practice is debugging plus engineering, not theorem-proving.
